title: Emergent Loop Geometry in Gauge-Equivariant Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Gauge-equivariant graph neural networks generate ordered products of gauge links through local message passing, but the geometry of these internal structures is not captured by the receptive field alone. We investigate the statistical ensemble of closed lattice walks generated by recursive node- and edge-feature operations, independently of network training. Analytical and numerical results reveal a separation between rapid growth of contour length and much slower spatial expansion: deeper compositions generate increasingly long paths through repeated traversal of relatively compact regions. Loop expansions of fermionic observables provide a physical interpretation of this hierarchy, showing how spatial locality remains compatible with high-order dependence on nearby gauge fields. These findings identify complementary roles of network depth in extending spatial reach and enriching the representations constructed within that reach, providing a geometrical perspective on learning lattice gauge observables.
summary: This paper investigates the emergent geometry of paths generated by gauge-equivariant Graph Neural Networks operating on lattice gauge theories. It finds a crucial separation where the total path length can grow exponentially while the physical spatial extent grows much more slowly. This suggests that deep network layers encode complex, highly redundant information within a relatively compact physical region.
main_problem: To understand the geometric structure of paths and loops generated by gauge-equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) through local message passing, which is not fully captured by the simple receptive field.
main_result: The analysis reveals a separation between the rapid, exponential growth of the total path length (contour length) and the much slower growth of the actual spatial extent of the generated loops.
method: The authors analyze the statistical ensemble of closed lattice walks generated by recursive node- and edge-feature operations within the GNN framework, independent of network training.
model_or_system: The model is based on lattice gauge configurations, relevant to non-Abelian gauge theories like QCD and condensed-matter systems such as quantum spin liquids. The GNN operates on a lattice structure using gauge-equivariant message passing.
key_observables: Contour length ($\ell$), Radius of Gyration ($	ext{Rg}$), Number of Distinct Visited Sites ($N_{	ext{distinct sites}}$), and Effective Dimension ($D_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Network depth ($n$), spatial dimension ($d=2, 3, 4$), and the gauge link variables $U_{ij} \in G$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the path generation process retains all ordered links, including immediately retraced ones, for accurate statistical counting.
figures_summary: Figure 8 plots geometric observables ($	ext{Rg}, N_{	ext{distinct sites}}, D_{	ext{eff}}$) against the total loop length ($\ell$) for various dimensions and recursion depths, visually confirming that length increases through repeated traversals within a slowly expanding spatial region.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the GNN mechanism for generating gauge-invariant loops, then analyzes the statistical properties of these paths by comparing contour length to spatial metrics, culminating in a physical interpretation via fermionic observable loop expansions.
why_interesting: The concept of path complexity diverging from simple spatial metrics is relevant to understanding entanglement structure or correlation functions in many-body systems where local interactions can lead to highly complex, non-local effective descriptions.
